KEY MESSAGE 1...Flood Watch issued for interior western New England, 
with heavy rainfall leading to potential street and flash flooding 
Tuesday afternoon through Wednesday evening. Heaviest rain in 
eastern New England is expected on Wednesday, with street flooding 
possible but less favored than further inland.

An anomalously strong upper-level cyclone for late July is expected 
to close off into a slow-moving upper low over central/south-central 
New York Tuesday into early Wed, then is forecast to slowly meander 
ESE through the lower Hudson Valley Wed into Wed night. This system 
will draw in rich subtropical moisture (e.g. PWAT values around 1.5-
1.7") along/ahead of a frontal boundary, a boundary will tend 
to slowly lift or pivot E/ENE Tue night/Wed. Additional 
enhancements to rainfall in an easterly upslope flow in interior
Southern New England are also anticipated. Put all that together
and we are looking at a soggy, dreary midweek with rounds of 
rainfall, some of which could turn heavy at times. Because of 
the slow eastward progression and timing, we'll break this down 
regionally below.

For interior portions of Southern New England: moderate to heavy 
rain with some embedded rumbles of thunder into expected to develop 
Tuesday afternoon and continue into Wednesday across western New 
England, especially into the CT Valley and northern CT. Heaviest 
rain is expected to fall late Tuesday night/overnight and continue 
into Wednesday. With a longer duration of this type of rain, 
the risk for street flooding as well as rises on creeks and 
streams looks to be the greatest in this general area. We've 
issued a Flood Watch to best message this potential for the CT 
Valley in MA into Hartford and Tolland Counties in CT, and this 
runs from Tuesday afternoon through early Wednesday evening. 
Although it is still uncertain what the maximum rainfall will 
be, this general area seems more primed to be at least in the 
vicinity of seeing that maximum; we'll also need to monitor 
where a pivot point ("deformation zone", in the weather 
vernacular) develops as the frontal boundary lifts northeastward
as an area potentially favorable for heavier rain 
accumulations. This is also reflected in the coarser-resolution 
global ensemble QPF probs from the ECMWF, Canadian GEM and the 
GEFS, which show high probs of 2+ inches of rainfall, with low 
(<20%) probs of 4 or more inches of rain. We're also not yet 
really into the higher- resolution guidance yet, so we still 
have to digest that data as we move through the next 24-36 
hours, but the synoptic-scale picture paints the potential for 
locally significant rainfall accumulations in western New 
England. This is also reflected in the ECMWF Extreme Forecast 
Index (EFI) and Shift of Tails guidance and justifies the Watch.
Although a slight risk for excessive rainfall was collaborated 
with WPC, a zone of moderate risk has now been introduced for 
points just to our south and west into the lower Hudson Valley 
in New York, which speaks to the risk for flooding. Additional, 
but lighter rain is expected even into Thursday. I've shown rain
totals through 7 AM Thursday which range from 2 to 3 inches, 
with locally higher totals nearing 4 inches along the east 
slopes of the Berkshires.

For eastern portions of Southern New England, roughly Worcester and 
Windham Counties eastward into RI and eastern MA: outside of 
isolated to widely scattered rain showers associated with a 
northward-moving warm front Tuesday morning, much of this region 
ends up being mostly dry on Tuesday with a relative minimum in PoPs 
(chance or less). The frontal boundary will be gradually moving in 
either late Tuesday night (after midnight), but more likely by early 
Wednesday. It looks like Wednesday is the period of moderate to 
heavier rainfall for this portion of Southern New England, only
slowly decreasing in intensity as we move into Wednesday
afternoon to early evening. There could be some risk for street
flooding here too, especially in the typically more vulnerable 
urban areas (not limited to Boston, Providence, Worcester, Fall 
River and New Bedford), but felt the risk was less than into 
western portions of Southern New England who are poised to see a
longer duration of moderate to heavy rain. Later shift(s) could
consider expanding the Flood Watch into some of these locations
if rain totals continue to increase, but it seems more 
conditional/marginal. Rain totals through 7 AM Thursday range 
from 1.5 to 2.5 inches, with the highest rainfall totals in 
hillier Worcester County as well as into the Merrimack Valley. 

In terms of river response...obviously one of the bigger challenges 
when it comes to projecting impacts is that we're still dealing with 
a stubborn drought where streamflows in several locations are still 
below-normal. Right now there are no rivers forecast to rise into
